content: Ovarian cancer is the seventh most commonly diagnosed cancer globally and ranks as the eighth leading cause of cancer-related deaths. Among the various types of ovarian cancer, epithelial ovarian cancer is the most prevalent, accounting for approximately 90% of cases. The standard initial treatment for epithelial ovarian cancer involves a combination of cytoreductive surgery and chemotherapy based on platinum and taxane agents. However, more than half of the women diagnosed with epithelial ovarian cancer will experience a recurrence of the disease. These patients often require additional chemotherapy and, over time, may develop resistance to platinum-based treatments. Currently, there is limited guidance on the use of chemotherapy agents, including taxanes, for women with recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer. In the UK, drugs such as paclitaxel, topotecan, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin hydrochloride, trabectedin, and gemcitabine are approved for use. However, their administration is left to the discretion of clinicians, who must discuss potential adverse effects with their patients. Taxanes can be administered in two different dosing schedules: a lower-dose weekly regimen or a higher-dose three-weekly regimen. These regimens differ in terms of their side effect profiles and potentially their effectiveness. Since recurrent disease is considered incurable, it is crucial to weigh the side effects, treatment schedules, and quality of life alongside the life-prolonging benefits of treatment. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and toxicity of different taxane monotherapy regimens in women with recurrent epithelial ovarian, tubal, or primary peritoneal cancer. A comprehensive search of databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, was conducted up to March 22, 2022. Additional searches of trial registries and grey literature did not yield any new studies. A total of 1,500 records were identified, and after removing duplicates, 1,374 records were screened. Of these, 24 studies underwent full-text review, and four randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the analysis. The four included RCTs were multicenter studies conducted in hospital settings. They involved 981 participants with recurrent epithelial ovarian, tubal, or primary peritoneal cancer. The median age of participants ranged from 56 to 62 years, and all had a World Health Organization (WHO) performance status of 0 to 2. The proportion of participants with serous histology ranged from 56% to 85%. Among the participants, 71% had platinum-sensitive relapse, while 29% had platinum-resistant relapse. Most participants (94.4%) were taxane-naive, while a small proportion (5.6%) had been previously treated with taxanes. None of the studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias based on the Cochrane risk of bias tool. The analysis found that there may be little or no difference in overall survival (OS) between weekly and three-weekly paclitaxel regimens, but the evidence is highly uncertain (risk ratio [RR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66 to 1.33; two studies, 263 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, there may be little or no difference in response rate (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.48; two studies, 263 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or progression-free survival (PFS) (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.52; two studies, 263 participants; very low-certainty evidence) between the two regimens, but again, the evidence is very uncertain. Differences in adverse events were observed between the weekly and three-weekly paclitaxel regimens. The weekly regimen may reduce the risk of neutropenia (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.95; two studies, 260 participants; low-certainty evidence) and alopecia (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.73; one study, 205 participants; low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no difference in neurotoxicity between the two regimens, but the evidence is very uncertain (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.45; two studies, 260 participants; very low-certainty evidence). When comparing different doses of paclitaxel in the three-weekly regimen, the higher dose of 250 mg/m² was associated with a greater risk of neurotoxicity compared to the lower dose of 175 mg/m² (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.80; one study, 330 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Quality-of-life data were not extractable from any of the included studies. In conclusion, weekly paclitaxel may reduce the risk of neutropenia and alopecia compared to the three-weekly regimen, although the certainty of this evidence is low. Weekly dosing may have little or no negative impact on response rate, PFS, or OS, but the evidence is very uncertain. For three-weekly regimens, a lower dose of 175 mg/m² may reduce the risk of neurotoxicity compared to a higher dose of 250 mg/m², with moderate confidence in this finding. These results suggest that weekly paclitaxel or a lower-dose three-weekly regimen could be considered to minimize toxicity without significantly compromising treatment efficacy, although the evidence remains uncertain.
